entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Francesco Zabarella (born c. 1360, Padua – died October 5, 1417, Konstanz) emerged as a preeminent Italian cardinal, canonist, and diplomat whose intellectual contributions profoundly shaped the resolution of the Western Schism and the development of conciliar theory in the early 15th century. A pivotal figure during a period of ecclesiastical crisis, his legal acumen and advocacy for church reform positioned him at the heart of efforts to restore unity to a divided papacy, impacting not only the Catholic Church but also the broader political landscape of late medieval Europe. His work bridged the gap between traditional papal authority and the burgeoning calls for conciliar governance, making him indispensable to understanding the era's ecclesiological debates.

Educated in law at Bologna and Florence, Zabarella rose quickly through academic ranks, becoming a professor of canon law at Padua by 1385, where he taught for over two decades. His magnum opus, the *Commentaria in Decretales*, meticulously analyzed papal decretals and became a standard text for generations of canon lawyers. Appointed Bishop of Florence in 1410 and elevated to cardinal by Antipope John XXIII in 1411, Zabarella played a crucial role at the Council of Constance (1414-1418). He served as a leading theological and legal advisor, advocating for the deposition of the three rival popes—Gregory XII, Benedict XIII, and John XXIII—and the election of a new, unified pope, Martin V, which he witnessed shortly before his death. His participation was instrumental in drafting the council's foundational decrees, *Haec Sancta* and *Frequens*.
